_readme: Korean dermocosmetic and body-care products for the K-beauty library, consumed by build-kbeauty-pages.cjs. Only products the author is confident exist and are well characterised. Cosmetic structure-function wording, no invented INCI or percentages, no medical advice — atopic dermatitis and hair loss are deferred to clinicians throughout.

products.name: Atobarrier 365 Cream
products.whatItIs: Aestura is Amorepacific's pharmacy-counter dermocosmetic brand, and Atobarrier 365 is the line everything else hangs off. The cream is dense and slightly waxy, built around ceramides, and sold in a wide tub because it is too thick to squeeze from a tube. 아토 (ato) in the name is Korean shorthand for atopy-prone skin — a retail category rather than a medical one. The formula's job is unglamorous: slow water loss, leave the surface feeling cushioned instead of tight.
products.whoItSuits: Dry, tight, flaky skin that objects to most new products — the sort that stings when an unfamiliar toner goes on. It earns its keep through a heated Korean winter. Oily and combination skin will usually find it heavy across the T-zone, though it still works as a night-only layer. If you have diagnosed atopic dermatitis, treat this as comfort care alongside what your dermatologist prescribes, never instead of it.
products.howToUse: Last step of the evening routine, over your serum, on skin left slightly damp. A pea-sized amount covers the face; press it in rather than rubbing it around. Mornings are fine too, but use less if sunscreen and makeup follow. Warm it between fingertips first — it spreads far better than it looks like it will.
products.watchOut: The wide-mouth tub means fingers go in repeatedly; use a clean spatula if that bothers you. Its thickness also makes it pill under sunscreen applied too soon after, so wait a minute. And the 아토 branding implies a great deal — this is a cosmetic moisturiser, and a genuine eczema flare is a matter for a clinician.

products.name: Atobarrier 365 Lotion
products.whatItIs: The lighter sibling of the Atobarrier 365 cream — the same ceramide-led idea in an emulsion that pours rather than scoops. In Korean routine language this sits where a Western routine would use a lotion: after essence, before anything occlusive. It is meant for people who want the line's cushioned finish without the weight, and for warmer months when the cream feels like too much on the face.
products.whoItSuits: Combination and normal skin that runs dry in patches, and dry skin during humid months. It also suits anyone building a deliberately short routine, since it can be the only moisturising step. Very dry or visibly flaking skin will get more out of the cream. Reactive skin generally tolerates it well, but patch-test on the jaw for a few days like anything else.
products.howToUse: After toner or essence, morning and evening, on damp skin. Two or three pumps for the face and neck. In winter you can use it as the hydrating layer and put the cream on top; in summer it is usually enough on its own. Sunscreen goes over it in the morning, once it has settled.
products.watchOut: People buy the lotion expecting cream-level richness and come away disappointed — it is genuinely lighter, and on very dry skin it will feel like it has evaporated by mid-afternoon. It is also a fairly plain formula: the appeal is reliability, not novel actives. If you want the barrier feel the line is known for, the cream is the product that delivers it.

products.name: Atobarrier 365 Hydro Essence
products.whatItIs: A water-gel essence from the Atobarrier line, positioned as the hydrating step before the lotion or cream. It is the lightest thing the range makes: a bouncy gel that sinks in quickly and leaves almost no film. The pitch is that skin marketed as barrier-compromised still wants water, not just lipids, and that a humectant layer under an occlusive one works better than either alone.
products.whoItSuits: Dehydrated skin of any type, including oily skin that feels tight after cleansing. It is a sensible entry point to the line if you have never used a ceramide product and are unsure how your skin will respond. Skin that is properly dry rather than dehydrated will need something over the top — used alone in a cold, dry room this will not hold.
products.howToUse: After cleansing and toner, morning and evening. A coin-sized amount, pressed in with the palms rather than dragged with fingertips. Follow with the lotion or cream while your skin is still slightly tacky, which is when the occlusive step does the most good. It layers under sunscreen without pilling if you give it thirty seconds.
products.watchOut: Humectant-heavy gels can feel drying in genuinely arid conditions if you leave them uncovered — the water goes somewhere, and in a dehumidified office it is not into your skin. Always put something over it. The name also invites the assumption that an essence is doing more than a toner; in this range the difference is texture and price, not a different order of ingredient.

products.name: Ceramide Ato Concentrate Cream
products.whatItIs: Illiyoon is Amorepacific's supermarket-tier family line, and this is the product that made it a household name in Korea. A thick, unfussy ceramide cream sold in a large tub at a price that assumes you will use it on faces, arms, children's legs and everything else. It is not trying to be clever. The value proposition is volume and a formula plain enough that most reactive skin gets on with it.
products.whoItSuits: Households, essentially — dry and sensitive skin that needs a lot of product applied often, and anyone who resents paying serum prices for a body moisturiser. It suits dry faces perfectly well. Oily skin will find it too rich for daytime facial use. As with anything carrying the 아토 (ato) label, atopy-prone skin under a doctor's care should treat it as adjunct comfort, not therapy.
products.howToUse: Apply generously wherever skin feels tight, ideally within a few minutes of a shower while the surface is still damp. On the face it is a night cream for most people. On limbs, twice a day in winter is not excessive. Because it is cheap by the tub, the usual mistake — using too little — is easy to avoid here.
products.watchOut: "Concentrate" is doing marketing work; there is no unusual technology inside, and that is fine — it is a competent basic ceramide cream, priced accordingly. Judge it on cost per application. The tub invites repeated finger-dipping, so decant if you are fussy. And read the current pack: Illiyoon has revised these formulas over the years, so an old review may not describe what you are buying.

products.name: Ceramide Ato Lotion
products.whatItIs: The pump-bottle body lotion version of Illiyoon's ceramide idea, sold in a bottle large enough to sit in a bathroom rather than on a dressing table. It is thinner than the concentrate cream and absorbs faster, which is what you want on arms and legs in the ninety seconds after a shower. In Korea it is a default winter purchase rather than a considered skincare decision, which tells you roughly what to expect.
products.whoItSuits: Anyone with dry, tight or rough-feeling body skin, particularly shins and forearms. It works for the whole family and is inoffensive enough for most reactive skin, though fragrance-sensitive users should check the current pack. If you want a body product that visibly softens texture through actives, this is not it — this is hydration and barrier comfort at a price that lets you be generous.
products.howToUse: Straight out of the shower, on skin patted rather than rubbed dry. Three or four pumps per limb; do not ration it. Reapply to shins and elbows in the evening during a cold snap. It can go on the face if that is what you have to hand, but a face-specific cream will suit a face better.
products.watchOut: It is formulated as body care, so it is heavier and less considered than a facial moisturiser — some people break out using it on the face. The 아토 naming again suggests more than a cosmetic can claim; for diagnosed eczema, comfort between medicated applications is the honest description, and the timing of that is a conversation with your clinician.

products.name: Red Blemish Clear Soothing Cream
products.whatItIs: Dr.G's best-known product and the one that built the brand's reputation with redness-prone skin. A gel-cream centred on centella asiatica — 병풀 (byeongpul) in Korean, the same plant sold everywhere as cica — aimed at skin that flushes easily and feels reactive after actives or sun. It sits somewhere between a light moisturiser and a comfort layer, and it has been on shelves long enough to be thoroughly characterised.
products.whoItSuits: Skin that goes pink for no obvious reason, or after retinoids, exfoliating acids and hot weather. Combination and normal skin will find the texture about right. It is a reasonable choice for acne-prone skin that wants moisture without a heavy cream. Very dry skin will want something richer over it. Anyone with persistent facial redness should get a diagnosis before assuming a cosmetic is the answer.
products.howToUse: Morning and evening as your moisturiser, after serum. It layers under sunscreen well, which is the main reason people keep it in a summer routine. On an irritated patch you can use it more heavily as a comfort layer at night. Give it a minute before makeup so it does not roll.
products.watchOut: The name misleads: "red blemish clear" reads like acne treatment, and there is nothing in here doing that job — no benzoyl peroxide, no acid, no retinoid. It calms the look of redness and moisturises. It is also thicker than the gel-cream description suggests, so very oily skin sometimes finds it sits on top rather than sinking in.

products.name: Red Blemish Clear Soothing Foam
products.whatItIs: The cleanser in Dr.G's Red Blemish range, built to the same brief as the cream: a mild wash for skin that reacts to most foaming cleansers. It lathers modestly rather than squeakily, which is the point — the aim is to remove sunscreen and sweat without stripping the surface. As the second cleanse in a Korean double-cleansing routine it does exactly what it is supposed to and no more.
products.whoItSuits: Reactive, easily-flushed skin that finds standard foaming cleansers leave a tight, shiny feeling afterwards. It works for combination and acne-prone skin too. Very dry skin may prefer a cream or milk cleanser. If your skin feels fine with whatever you already use, there is no argument for switching — cleansers are the step where upgrading changes the least.
products.howToUse: Second step of an evening double cleanse, after an oil or balm has taken off sunscreen and makeup. A short pump's worth, emulsified in wet hands first, then thirty seconds on the face and a thorough rinse. Mornings, use it only if your skin feels congested on waking; water alone is often enough.
products.watchOut: This is a rinse-off product, so the centella in it has seconds of contact time and does very little. Buy it because it is a gentle wash, not because of the calming claim on the front. The wider trap is the range name again — nothing here treats blemishes, and a cleanser has never been where acne is won or lost.

products.name: Green Mild Up Sun+
products.whatItIs: Dr.G's sunscreen for reactive skin, sold under the brand's green dermocosmetic positioning and carrying a high SPF with PA++++ for UVA. It is the sun step most people meet Dr.G through after the soothing cream. The formula is pitched at skin that stings with conventional sunscreens, and it wears more like a light moisturiser than a beach product, which is the whole reason Korean sunscreens travel so well.
products.whoItSuits: Sensitive and normal skin that wants daily protection it will not resent applying. It suits redness-prone faces well and sits reasonably under makeup. Very oily skin may want something drier-finishing; very dry skin may want a cream underneath. Anyone who has reacted to a specific UV filter before should read the current filter list on the pack rather than trusting the word "mild".
products.howToUse: Final step of the morning routine, after moisturiser, before makeup. The standard measurement guidance is roughly two finger-lengths for face and neck, and most people apply far less than that. Reapply every couple of hours outdoors. Give it two or three minutes to set before anything goes over the top.
products.watchOut: "Mild" is a marketing word with no regulatory meaning, and plenty of people with reactive skin still find sunscreens uncomfortable around the eyes. Formulas and filter lists also change between production runs and export markets, so the tube you buy abroad may not match the review you read. Apply enough or the SPF number on the front is fiction.

products.name: Dual Barrier Cream
products.whatItIs: Celimax is an indie Korean brand that undercuts the pharmacy lines on price while chasing the same barrier-care brief. The Dual Barrier Cream is its clearest expression of that: a moderately rich cream sold on the idea of supporting both the skin's water-holding and its lipid layers at once. It is a competent, unshowy formula in the same family as the Aestura and Illiyoon creams, at a lower entry price.
products.whoItSuits: Dry and sensitive skin on a budget, and anyone who wants to try ceramide-style barrier care without committing to a large tub. Combination skin can use it at night. Oily skin will find it more than it needs. It is a sensible first purchase if you are unsure whether your problem is dryness or dehydration, because it addresses the feeling of both.
products.howToUse: Final step at night, over serum, on damp skin. A pea to a hazelnut for the face depending on the season. Mornings are fine in winter, though a lighter emulsion suits most people under sunscreen. If your skin is flaking, apply, wait ten minutes and apply a second thin layer to the worst patches.
products.watchOut: "Dual barrier" is a phrase Celimax coined, not a technical category — no one else uses it and it describes an intention rather than a mechanism. Indie brands also reformulate more often and with less notice than the big houses, so check the ingredient list on the pack in front of you rather than assuming continuity with an older batch.

products.name: The Real Noni Energy Ampoule
products.whatItIs: Celimax's most exported product: a lightweight ampoule built around noni fruit extract, sold as a hydrating and comforting layer rather than a treatment. 앰플 (aempul) in Korean marketing simply means a concentrated liquid step; it carries no fixed technical definition and no minimum active content. This one is slippery, sinks in fast and layers well, which is most of why people repurchase it.
products.whoItSuits: Dehydrated skin that wants an extra water layer without weight, and people who like the Korean habit of a thin liquid step between toner and moisturiser. It is gentle enough for most reactive skin. If you are shopping for a serum that will visibly change pigmentation, texture or fine lines, this is not that product and does not really claim to be.
products.howToUse: After toner, before moisturiser, morning and evening. Three or four drops pressed into damp skin. It layers under heavier creams without pilling and works well as a mid-step in the Korean seven-skin habit, where thin hydrating layers are applied repeatedly rather than one thick one. Always seal it with something.
products.watchOut: Noni is the marketing hook and the topical evidence behind it is thin — treat this as a pleasant humectant layer and you will not be disappointed. The word "energy" means nothing. It is also worth being clear that an ampoule at this price is not more concentrated than a serum by any regulated standard; the naming is a texture and positioning choice.

products.name: Essence Toner
products.whatItIs: Pyunkang Yul grew out of a Korean herbal medicine clinic, and its house style is short ingredient lists and no fragrance. The Essence Toner is the product that made the brand internationally: a slightly viscous, almost weightless liquid with a famously brief formula led by coptis root extract. It is a hydrating first step rather than an astringent toner in the old Western sense, and it has been widely reviewed for years.
products.whoItSuits: Reactive, easily-irritated skin, and anyone who wants to strip a routine back to find out what was actually causing trouble. It suits dry and combination skin, and oily skin that dislikes the film most toners leave. If you are looking for a toner that exfoliates or brightens, look at a tonerpad or an acid formula instead — this deliberately does one thing.
products.howToUse: Straight after cleansing, on damp skin, morning and evening. Pour into the palms and press in; cotton pads waste it. Two or three thin layers in sequence is the Korean way to use it and works better than one heavy one. Follow with an ampoule or moisturiser while the skin is still slightly tacky.
products.watchOut: A short ingredient list is read online as proof of gentleness, and it is not — a formula is only as gentle as its individual ingredients, and short lists can still contain something that suits you badly. The texture is also slightly slippery in a way some people dislike, and this genuinely does very little beyond hydrate. That is the point, but manage expectations.

products.name: Moisture Ampoule
products.whatItIs: The concentrated hydration step in Pyunkang Yul's minimal line, following the same house rules as the Essence Toner: short list, no fragrance, nothing dramatic. It is thicker than the toner and thinner than a cream, designed to be the layer that holds water in place before an occlusive goes on. The brand's appeal is consistency — you broadly know what you are getting across the range.
products.whoItSuits: Dry and dehydrated skin that reacts to fragranced or busy formulas, and anyone assembling a deliberately boring routine while their skin settles down. Combination skin can use it year-round. Oily skin may find it enough on its own in summer. It is not the right purchase if you want a targeted active for pigmentation, acne or fine lines.
products.howToUse: After the toner, before moisturiser, morning and evening. A few drops, pressed rather than rubbed, on skin that is still damp. In winter, layer it under a ceramide cream; in summer it can be the last step for oilier skin. It sits under sunscreen without pilling if you let it absorb properly.
products.watchOut: The word ampoule promises potency that the category does not guarantee — in Korean retail it describes a texture and a position in the routine, nothing more. This is a hydrating layer, priced fairly for what it is. If you already use a good hydrating toner and a decent moisturiser, adding it is a comfort upgrade rather than a meaningful change to your routine.

products.name: ATO Cream Blue Label
products.whatItIs: Pyunkang Yul's ATO range is its line for atopy-prone and highly reactive skin, sold in clinical blue-and-white packaging that deliberately signals pharmacy rather than beauty counter. The cream is rich, plain and fragrance-free, intended for face and body alike and for skin of any age, including children's. It follows the brand's minimal-formula approach, which is the main reason it appears in so many Korean parents' bathroom cupboards.
products.whoItSuits: Very dry, tight or persistently flaky skin, and skin that has reacted to fragranced moisturisers before. It suits face and body, and it is commonly used on children — though a paediatrician or dermatologist should guide anything applied regularly to a child with an atopic diagnosis. Oily and combination skin will find it heavier than it needs on the face.
products.howToUse: Apply liberally to damp skin after washing, morning and night, concentrating on shins, forearms and anywhere that feels rough. On the face, an evening layer over your usual hydrating step. Reapply through the day on hands and any patch that starts to feel tight. Generosity matters more than technique with a product like this.
products.watchOut: The blue clinical packaging and the ATO name read as medicine and this is a cosmetic — it moisturises and makes skin feel more comfortable, and that is the honest ceiling. Atopic dermatitis is a medical condition with medical treatments, and using an emollient instead of prescribed care is how flares get worse. Ask your clinician where a cream like this fits.

products.name: ATO Wash & Shampoo Blue Label
products.whatItIs: A combined body wash and shampoo from Pyunkang Yul's ATO line, formulated for atopy-prone skin and low-lathering by design. Korean atopy-branded washes avoid the aggressive surfactants that make conventional shower gels feel squeaky, on the reasoning that the shower is where a lot of dryness is manufactured in the first place. Fragrance-free, mild, and intended for the whole family including the 두피 (dupi), the scalp.
products.whoItSuits: Dry, tight, itchy-feeling skin that gets worse after showering, and households that want one bottle for everyone. It suits children's skin, again with a clinician's input if there is a diagnosis. People with oily scalps or heavy styling-product use will find it does not clean thoroughly enough, and anyone with a diagnosed scalp condition needs a medicated shampoo, not this.
products.howToUse: Use in a short, warm — not hot — shower. Work a small amount into wet hair at the scalp and let the run-off do the body, or apply directly to dry-feeling areas. Rinse well and pat dry, then moisturise within a few minutes while skin is still damp. That last step is where most of the benefit actually comes from.
products.watchOut: Two-in-one products are a compromise and this is no exception: it is a gentle wash that happens to be usable on hair, not a good shampoo. Expect very little lather, which people misread as the product not working. And a mild wash does nothing for seborrhoeic dermatitis, psoriasis or persistent scalp itching — those need a diagnosis and, usually, a medicated product.

products.name: Ceramidin Cream
products.whatItIs: Dr.Jart+ built the international idea of Korean derma-cosmetics, and Ceramidin is its barrier line. The cream is thick, faintly balmy and centred on a blend of ceramides, sold in a tub with a spatula and priced well above the Korean pharmacy equivalents. It has been reformulated more than once over its life, so it is worth reading the current pack rather than a review from several years ago.
products.whoItSuits: Dry, tight and mature skin, particularly through winter, and anyone whose skin feels rough despite using a moisturiser twice a day. It suits sensitive skin, though fragrance-avoidant users should check the current list. Oily and combination skin will find it excessive except as an occasional overnight layer. Acne-prone skin should introduce it slowly on a small area first.
products.howToUse: Last step at night, over serum, on skin left damp. A small scoop for the face; the spatula exists so you can be honest about how much you are using. In very dry conditions, apply a second thin layer to cheeks and around the nose. Mornings work in winter, though it can be heavy under sunscreen.
products.watchOut: The honest problem is value. This is a good ceramide cream, but Aestura, Illiyoon and Celimax sell the same category for a fraction of the price per millilitre, and blind preference between them tends to come down to texture rather than results. Buy it because you like how it feels, not because the price implies a better class of ingredient.

products.name: Ceramidin Liquid
products.whatItIs: The first step of the Ceramidin routine: a thin, milky liquid that behaves like a hydrating toner but carries the line's ceramide angle. Korean routines use a watery first step to prepare skin for everything after it, and this is Dr.Jart+'s version, slightly richer than a plain toner and slightly more slippery. It is best understood as a hydrating layer with a barrier-flavoured story attached.
products.whoItSuits: Dry and sensitive skin that finds conventional toners drying, and people who like the Korean layering habit. Combination skin will get on with it fine. Oily skin can use it, though cheaper hydrating toners do a comparable job. If your skin is currently comfortable, this is an optional addition rather than a missing step.
products.howToUse: Immediately after cleansing, on damp skin, morning and evening. Pour into the palms and press it in — two or three thin passes rather than one soaking. Follow with serum and the cream while skin still feels slightly tacky. Most people under-apply liquids like this; a properly covered face takes more than you think.
products.watchOut: A ceramide in a rinse-adjacent watery step is doing much less than the same ingredient in a cream that stays put, so treat this as hydration first and barrier care a distant second. It is also expensive for a toner. If the budget is finite, put the money into the cream and use a plain hydrating toner underneath — you will not notice the difference.

products.name: Ceramidin Body Lotion
products.whatItIs: The body version of Dr.Jart+'s ceramide line — a rich lotion aimed at the shins, forearms and hands that get rough every winter. Ceramide body care is a well-established Korean category rather than a novelty, and this is the premium end of it: nicer to use than most, with the texture and finish you would expect at the price. It absorbs faster than the face cream despite being generously emollient.
products.whoItSuits: Dry, rough or flaky body skin, especially anyone who showers daily in hard water or spends winter in heated rooms. It suits sensitive skin, though check the current pack if you avoid fragrance entirely. Anyone treating body skin on a budget should compare it honestly with the large-format Korean ceramide lotions, which cost far less per application.
products.howToUse: Apply within a few minutes of showering, on skin patted dry but still slightly damp — that window is when a body lotion does the most. Concentrate on shins, elbows and forearms. Reapply to hands after washing them. In a cold snap, a second evening application on the legs is more useful than switching to a richer product.
products.watchOut: Cost per use is the sticking point. Body skin needs a lot of product, and the maths on a premium body lotion rarely favours the buyer over a large pump bottle of the same ingredient class. It is a pleasant product, not a materially better one. If you find yourself rationing it to make the bottle last, you are using it wrong and should buy something cheaper.

products.name: Cicapair Tiger Grass Cream
products.whatItIs: The cream that made cica a global shelf category. Cicapair is built on centella asiatica — marketed in English as tiger grass — and pitched at skin that flushes, stings and reacts. The cream is a mid-weight moisturiser with a slightly green-grey cast in the tub that disappears on the skin. It has been on sale long enough, and copied often enough, to be one of the best-characterised products in Korean derma-cosmetics.
products.whoItSuits: Skin that reddens easily, or that has been pushed too hard with acids and retinoids and needs a few quiet weeks. Combination and normal skin will find the weight about right. Very dry skin will want something over it. Persistent facial redness — rosacea in particular — is a medical matter, and a soothing cream is at best a comfort measure alongside proper treatment.
products.howToUse: Morning or evening as the moisturising step, after serum. A pea-sized amount for the face, pressed in. It sits under sunscreen and makeup acceptably once it has settled for a minute. During a reactive spell, cutting your routine back to cleanser, this and sunscreen for a fortnight is more useful than adding anything else.
products.watchOut: The tiger grass origin story — tigers supposedly rolling in the plant to soothe wounds — is folklore doing marketing work, and centella's cosmetic evidence, while decent for the appearance of redness, does not support the drama. The range also has a confusing number of near-identical products. Pick one and ignore the rest; buying three Cicapair items is the classic mistake.

products.name: Cicapair Tiger Grass Color Correcting Treatment
products.whatItIs: The famous one: a green cream that turns beige on contact with skin as encapsulated pigment breaks under pressure. It is a colour-correcting base with a centella story attached, sold as skincare and behaving mostly like a very light complexion product. The green-to-beige transformation is the reason it goes viral every couple of years, and it is a pigment mechanism, not skincare working in front of your eyes.
products.whoItSuits: People who want to knock back the look of visible redness without wearing foundation, on a fairly narrow band of light-to-medium skin tones. It suits normal and combination skin best. Deeper skin tones are not well served — the beige it turns is essentially one shade. Dry skin should moisturise properly underneath, as it can cling to flaking patches.
products.howToUse: After moisturiser, as the last step before makeup or on its own. A small amount, dotted and blended with fingers rather than rubbed in hard — pressure is what triggers the colour shift, so work it in fully or you will have green edges. Remove it properly at night with an oil or balm cleanser.
products.watchOut: Two things. The colour change is theatre, not efficacy: it is doing what a tinted cream does. And some versions carry an SPF rating that people rely on as their only sun protection — you will never apply enough of a cosmetic base to get the labelled figure, so wear an actual sunscreen underneath and treat any SPF here as a bonus.

products.name: SoonJung 2x Barrier Intensive Cream
products.whatItIs: SoonJung — 순정 (sunjeong), roughly "pure and gentle" — is ETUDE's line for reactive skin, and this cream is its centrepiece. The formula is built around panthenol and madecassoside, keeps the ingredient count low, and skips fragrance and colourant. It is one of the cheapest genuinely well-formulated barrier creams on the international market, which is why it turns up in so many dermatology-adjacent recommendation lists.
products.whoItSuits: Sensitive skin that reacts to most things, skin recovering from over-exfoliation, and anyone starting a retinoid who needs a buffer. Dry and normal skin will like the weight; combination skin can use it at night. Oily skin often finds it too rich for daytime. It is also a sensible cream for people who react to fragrance, which rules out a great deal of the market.
products.howToUse: Evening, as the last step, on damp skin over your serum. A pea-sized amount, pressed in. If you are using a retinoid, applying this first as a buffer and again on top is a well-worn way to reduce the sting in the early weeks. Mornings work in cold weather, under sunscreen, if you use less.
products.watchOut: The "2x" refers to nothing measurable and no standard defines it. The texture is also genuinely rich — it looks like a light cream in the tube and behaves like a heavier one on the face, so oily skin frequently finds it sits on the surface. And a barrier cream is comfort and prevention: if your skin is actively inflamed and not settling, that is a dermatologist's territory.

products.name: SoonJung pH 5.5 Relief Toner
products.whatItIs: The hydrating first step of the SoonJung line, formulated at a mildly acidic pH close to the skin's own surface and kept free of fragrance and colourant. It is a plain, watery toner with panthenol doing most of the work — no acids, no astringents, nothing to react to. In a routine being stripped back after a bout of irritation, this is the sort of product that gets kept while everything else is removed.
products.whoItSuits: Reactive and dehydrated skin of any type, including oily skin that has been over-cleansed. It is a good default toner for teenagers and for anyone whose skin has recently rebelled against an active. If you want a toner that exfoliates, brightens or does anything measurable to texture, this is the wrong product and deliberately so.
products.howToUse: Straight after cleansing, on damp skin, morning and evening. Press it in with the palms; a cotton pad soaks up most of it for no benefit unless you specifically want the wiping action. Two thin layers beat one heavy one. Follow with serum and moisturiser before it fully dries — that is when layering actually helps.
products.watchOut: "Relief" oversells it. This hydrates and is unlikely to annoy your skin, which is a genuine virtue, but it does not calm anything on its own. The large plastic bottle has a wide opening that pours too fast, so expect to waste some. And a pH figure on the front is only meaningful for products that stay on or wash off — for a toner it is reassurance more than function.

products.name: SoonJung pH 6.5 Whip Cleanser
products.whatItIs: A soft, low-foaming cleanser from the SoonJung line, formulated without fragrance or colourant and built to leave skin feeling comfortable rather than squeaky. The whipped texture is the selling point — it comes out somewhere between a cream and a foam and spreads without needing much water. It is inexpensive, widely available and has been a standing recommendation for reactive skin for years.
products.whoItSuits: Sensitive and dry skin that finds most foaming washes leave a tight film, and anyone whose skin has been irritated by a strong cleanser. Normal and combination skin will find it perfectly adequate. Very oily skin, or anyone wearing heavy sunscreen and makeup, will need an oil or balm cleanse first — this is not built to shift that alone.
products.howToUse: Second cleanse in the evening, after an oil or balm. A small amount, worked in with wet hands for about thirty seconds, then rinsed thoroughly with lukewarm water. In the morning, use it only if you wake up oily; otherwise water is fine. Moisturise while your face is still damp.
products.watchOut: The number on the front is worth reading properly: pH 6.5 is milder than a traditional soap-based foam but it is not low-pH, and healthy skin sits more acidic than that. It is a gentle cleanser, not an acid-balanced one. The whipped texture also encourages over-dispensing — a small blob is plenty, and using three times as much is just a shorter-lived tube.

products.name: SoonJung Panthensoside Cica Balm
products.whatItIs: The comfort layer of the SoonJung line, combining the panthenol the range is built on with centella derivatives. ETUDE calls the blend Panthensoside, which is a brand name rather than an ingredient category. Despite "balm" in the title it is closer to a rich cream than an ointment — it presses in and disappears rather than sitting on the surface like a salve, and it is fragrance-free like the rest of the line.
products.whoItSuits: Skin having a bad week: post-exfoliation tightness, wind-burnt cheeks, the flat patches left after a spot has gone. It suits sensitive and dry skin, and combination skin can use it in targeted patches rather than all over. Oily skin will find full-face use heavy. It is a soothing cosmetic, so anything genuinely inflamed or persistent goes to a clinician, not to a balm.
products.howToUse: As the last step at night on the areas that need it, over serum, or all over the face if your skin is dry. It also works as a targeted patch treatment on rough spots during the day. Use less than you think — it looks thick in the tub and spreads a long way once warmed between the fingers.
products.watchOut: "Balm" sets the wrong expectation. If you are after a genuinely occlusive ointment for cracked, weeping or badly compromised skin, this is not dense enough and you should be asking a pharmacist or doctor instead. It is also easy to over-apply into a tacky film. And the Panthensoside name is proprietary — do not go looking for it on other brands' ingredient lists.

products.name: Rosemary Scalp Scaling Shampoo
products.whatItIs: Aromatica is a Korean natural-cosmetics brand and this is its best-known export — a sulfate-free shampoo aimed at the 두피 (dupi), the scalp, rather than at hair length. "Scaling" is Korean scalp-care vocabulary for a deeper clean that lifts buildup. It smells strongly of rosemary and mint, lathers less than a conventional shampoo, and is used more like a scalp treatment that happens to wash hair.
products.whoItSuits: Oily or buildup-prone scalps, people who use a lot of dry shampoo or styling product, and anyone whose scalp feels heavy by the second day. It suits colour-treated hair better than sulfate shampoos do. Dry, coarse or curly hair will find the length left thirsty. If your scalp itches, flakes persistently or is sore, see a dermatologist rather than shopping.
products.howToUse: Wet hair thoroughly, apply directly to the scalp in sections and massage with fingertips — never nails — for a minute or two. Rinse very well; sulfate-free formulas need more rinsing than people expect. Condition mid-lengths and ends only. Two washes are sometimes needed on the first use if there is a lot of buildup.
products.watchOut: The rosemary-grows-hair claim has run far ahead of the evidence. A small clinical comparison is endlessly cited online, and it is thin ground for what the internet has built on top of it — a shampoo has minutes of contact time regardless. The mint tingle also stings if it reaches your eyes, and hair loss is a medical question that deserves a proper diagnosis.

products.name: Rosemary Root Enhancer
products.whatItIs: A leave-on scalp tonic from Aromatica's rosemary line, sold as the step after the shampoo for people who want to keep going. It is a thin liquid applied directly to the scalp and left in, scented like the rest of the range. Korean scalp care treats the scalp as skin with its own routine — cleanse, tone, treat — and this is the treat step in that framing.
products.whoItSuits: People with oily or congested scalps who already like the shampoo and want a leave-on layer, and anyone who enjoys a scalp massage routine in the evening. It suits most hair types since it stays at the roots. Dry or sensitive scalps should patch-test behind one ear first, as leave-on tonics are the products most likely to sting.
products.howToUse: On a towel-dried or dry scalp, part the hair in sections and apply a small amount along each parting. Massage in with the fingertips for a minute. Evening is easier than morning because it needs to dry. Do not rinse. Once daily is plenty; more frequently is where irritation tends to start.
products.watchOut: This is a cosmetic scalp product and the expectation gap around it is enormous. Nothing here is a hair-loss treatment, the evidence for rosemary in that role is much weaker than social media suggests, and pattern hair loss has actual medical options that work — a dermatologist is the right first call. If a leave-on tonic stings, tightens or flakes the scalp, stop using it.
